name: Irish Coffee
intro: Irish coffee is hot coffee spiked with Irish whiskey and a little brown sugar, crowned with a layer of lightly whipped cream. You drink the hot coffee through the cool cream, which is half the fun. It's warming, rich and a little bit festive.
heroAlt: Engraved line illustration of Irish coffee with cream

vessel.name: Stemmed Irish coffee glass or heatproof mug
vessel.note: Warm the glass first so it doesn't crack or cool the drink.

ingredients.note: Whipped just until it thickens but still pours, so it floats.

equipment.item: Coffee maker or any brewing method
equipment.alternative: French press, pour-over or moka pot
Handheld frother or shake in a sealed jar

steps.title: Warm the glass
steps.body: Fill the glass with hot water for a minute, then empty it. A warm glass keeps the drink hot longer and helps prevent thermal shock.
steps.tip: Use a heatproof glass designed for hot drinks.

steps.title: Whip the cream
steps.body: Whisk cold cream just until it thickens slightly but is still pourable, like softly flowing lotion. Lightly whipped cream floats on the coffee, while stiff cream sinks or clumps.
steps.tip: Shaking cream in a sealed jar for 30 to 60 seconds also works. Check often.

steps.title: Brew strong coffee
steps.body: Brew about 4 oz of hot, strong coffee. It needs to hold its own against the whiskey and cream, so use a bold roast and fresh grounds.

steps.title: Dissolve the sugar
steps.body: Add 1 tsp of brown sugar to the glass, pour in the hot coffee, and stir until completely dissolved. Brown sugar adds a hint of molasses that pairs well with whiskey.
steps.tip: Undissolved sugar sinks to the bottom, so stir well.

steps.title: Add the whiskey
steps.body: Stir in 1½ oz of Irish whiskey. Adding it to the hot coffee blends the flavors, though some alcohol will soften with heat.

steps.title: Float the cream
steps.body: Hold the back of a spoon just above the surface and pour the cream gently over it so it floats in a layer. Don't stir. Sip the coffee through the cream.
steps.tip: Pour slowly and keep the spoon low for a clean layer.

homeMethods.note: This is the standard home method. A strong, fresh brew is all you need. Irish coffee is traditionally made with regular brewed coffee, not espresso.
Gives a rich, full-bodied cup that holds up well to whiskey and cream. Brew it a little stronger than usual.
A moka pot brew diluted to about 4 oz works. It's bolder and a bit more intense than drip coffee.

tips: Fresh, hot coffee matters. Cold or stale coffee makes a flat drink.
Chill the cream and bowl for easier whipping.
Whiskey brands vary in sweetness and flavor, so choose one you enjoy.
Recipes vary by bar and region, and some use different sweeteners.
commonMistakes: Over-whipping the cream so it won't float.
Using weak coffee that disappears behind the whiskey.
Skipping the glass warm-up and serving a lukewarm drink.

variations.name: Baileys coffee
variations.description: Uses Irish cream liqueur, giving a sweeter, creamier drink. It's a different drink from traditional Irish coffee.

variations.name: Decaf Irish coffee
variations.description: Use decaf for an evening version.

variations.name: Alcohol-free version
variations.description: Skip the whiskey and add a drop of vanilla or a splash of non-alcoholic whiskey alternative.

history: Irish coffee is commonly credited to Joe Sheridan, a chef at Foynes airport in Ireland, in the 1940s. It was later popularized in the US, notably at a San Francisco bar in the 1950s. Details of the story vary between tellings.

seo.title: How to Make Irish Coffee: Whiskey, Coffee and Cream
seo.description: Make a classic Irish coffee with 1½ oz Irish whiskey, brown sugar, hot coffee and lightly whipped cream. Step-by-step guide with tips for floating the cream.
